summary: At three people per square mile, Sierra County is one of the least densely populated counties in the entire continental United States — its 961 square miles hold fewer residents than a single large apartment complex in San Francisco. This is rugged northern Sierra Nevada terrain, heavily forested with pine and fir, cut through by the North Yuba and Middle Fork Feather rivers, and climbing to peaks above 8,000 feet. The county seat of Downieville, a Gold Rush-era town tucked into a river canyon, doubles as a world-class mountain biking destination, drawing riders to its steep, technical singletrack each summer. With a median home value of $334,100 against a median household income of $60,000, the price-to-income ratio sits around 5.6× — meaningful but far below California's coastal markets — though the practical challenge is inventory: there simply aren't many homes changing hands in a county of 3,100 people. There is no major employer base; government services and tourism-adjacent businesses anchor the economy, and almost any professional-sector job requires a long, winding mountain commute. Winters average lows around 36°F with heavy snowfall at elevation, while summers bring nine hours of sunshine and dry, clear days ideal for trail access. Sierra County offers genuine remoteness in a state where that commodity is vanishing — but remoteness and convenience are, by definition, the same tradeoff.
